ServiceNow for FinOps Collapse All What is FinOps? Cloud computing has revolutionized the way organizations operate, offering unparalleled flexibility, scalability, and efficiency. The ability to access on-demand resources and dynamically adjust infrastructure has empowered businesses to rapidly innovate and adapt to changing market demands even as they occur. However, not every venture into the cloud yields the expected success, particularly when it comes to managing costs. Cloud operational management typically involves multiple teams and departments, leading to decentralized decision-making and fragmented cost control. The distributed nature of cloud spending makes it challenging for organizations to predict and control expenses effectively. Consequently, businesses frequently find themselves grappling with soaring cloud costs that can easily hinder growth, strain budgets, and undermine the advantages inherent in cloud computing. In the pursuit of more dependable financial control and optimization in the cloud, organizations have turned to cloud FinOps. This comprehensive methodology for managing cloud costs bridges the gap between finance, operations, and cloud management, providing a framework to tackle the complexities of cloud spending and maximize the value derived from cloud investments. Bring Your Own License Leverage on-premises software licenses by bringing them to public clouds Get Ebook What is the Focus of FinOps? More than anything, FinOps is the recognition and acceptance that traditional infrastructure and cost management is simply not effective when working within the cloud. To this end, FinOps solutions focus on: Efficiency Efficiency lies at the heart of FinOps. Wasting money is detrimental to any business, and to thrive, organizations must utilize their resources judiciously, extracting the maximum value from every dollar spent. FinOps encourages businesses to adopt a proactive approach to cost management, identifying areas of waste and inefficiency to optimize resource allocation and eliminate unnecessary expenditure. Optimization By continuously striving to do more with less, organizations can uncover cost-saving opportunities, leverage automation, and streamline workflows. FinOps empowers teams to identify optimal resource configurations, implement cost-effective strategies, and align cloud spending with business goals, ensuring a sustainable and cost-efficient cloud environment. Three key areas of optimization would include cloud computing, storage, and databases. Continuous Improvement Learning from both mistakes and successes is a fundamental aspect of achieving financial excellence. FinOps emphasizes a culture of continuous improvement by leveraging real-time data and insights to refine financial processes. By monitoring, analyzing, and evaluating cloud costs on an ongoing basis, organizations can gain valuable intelligence that informs strategic decision-making. This iterative approach allows businesses to adapt to evolving requirements, enhance cost visibility, and foster collaboration between finance, operations, and development teams. How does FinOps work? FinOps brings together business, finance, and technology to optimize cloud- vendor management. FinOps is as much a cultural practice as a financial one; it establishes best practices for cloud usage and then relies on everyone involved to take ownership and be accountable for the expenses. Instead of individual, separate procurement teams working in silos to identify and approve costs, FinOps unites cross-functional teams of business, finance, and technology to better manage cloud vendors, rates, and available discounts in a cloud environment. When coupled with reliable real-time data, this provides increased financial and operational control. What is the origin of FinOps? Unlike many modern tech movements, FinOps is not a single advancement or policy change pioneered by any specific company or organization; it's a natural evolution of technology management to account for on-demand cloud resources. With the rise and proliferation of cloud computing, many companies began to see a shift from standard, traditional pricing to usage-based pricing models. And, while this allowed businesses to take a more cost-effective approach to technology—paying only for the time and resources they used, rather than paying a set rate—it created a crisis for CFOs. After all, it's next to impossible to predict tool usage with any degree of accuracy, which can make budgeting an exercise in futility. To address this issue, prevent runaway expenses, and promote business profitability, organizations around the world began to develop the concept of financial operations, (FinOps). This revolution was guided by respected technology companies around the world, first taking shape as cloud cost management, developing into cloud cost optimization, and then into cloud financial management. Finally, taking inspiration from the success of DevOps, FinOps was born, bringing cross-functionality and agility to financial management of cloud technologies. What are the 3 tenets of FinOps? To effectively assist organizations in better tracking and governing their cloud-related finances, FinOps is built on three essential tenets: Cost Optimization FinOps practitioners employ automation tools and cloud cost management solutions to identify opportunities for cost reduction and eliminate wasteful spending. By leveraging insights such as rightsizing recommendations, workload scheduling, and reservation planning, organizations can optimize their cloud resource usage and take advantage of discounts offered by cloud providers. Forecasting The ability to accurately predict future cloud costs is crucial for budgeting and resource allocation. While cloud providers offer their own consumption data and billing information, organizations may opt for dedicated FinOps and cloud financial management solutions to achieve a more unified view of the data across multiple clouds. Such solutions enable better understanding of cloud costs, enhance cost analyses, and facilitate increased forecasting accuracy. Accounting FinOps practitioners establish comprehensive processes and workflows to ensure accurate accounting of cloud expenses. They continuously evaluate business metrics, align cloud usage with business objectives, and define policies to optimize the value derived from the cloud. Proper accounting practices enable organizations to measure the financial impact of their cloud investments, align costs with specific projects or departments, and make informed decisions for future resource allocation. What is the goal of FinOps? By employing a collaborative approach that brings together finance, operations, and engineering teams, FinOps enables organizations to achieve several key goals. These goals include: Accelerating business value realization and innovation The primary goal of FinOps is to foster innovation while lowering the cost of doing business. By effectively managing cloud costs and resources, organizations can more strategically allocate their financial resources. FinOps leaders work closely with stakeholders to ensure that cloud investments align with business goals, allowing for the efficient deployment of resources and faster time-to-market for new products and services. Through proper cost optimization and budget allocation, FinOps empowers organizations to invest in innovative projects, drive revenue growth, and gain a competitive edge. Driving financial accountability and visibility Financial accountability and visibility are critical aspects of FinOps. Organizations need a clear understanding of their cloud costs and how they relate to various projects, teams, and departments. FinOps establishes processes, tools, and policies that provide detailed cost transparency, enabling stakeholders to take direct ownership of their cloud spending. By promoting financial accountability, FinOps encourages responsible cloud resource usage and cost-conscious decision-making, and gives users the ability to track the financial impact of cloud initiatives. Optimizing cloud usage and cost efficiency Cost optimization and efficiency are fundamental goals of FinOps. Organizations strive to optimize how they use cloud resources to ensure they are obtaining the maximum value from their investments. Through rightsizing, workload scheduling, and leveraging discounted pricing options, FinOps practitioners identify areas where costs may be reduced while eliminating unnecessary or underutilized resources. Enabling cross-organizational trust and collaboration FinOps fosters cross-organizational trust and collaboration by breaking down silos between finance, operations, and engineering teams, aligning interests, and creating a shared understanding of cloud costs and their impact on business outcomes. This promotes collaboration and effective communication, encouraging stakeholders to work together, exchange insights, and make decisions that balance financial considerations with operational needs. Preventing cloud sprawl Cloud sprawl, or uncontrolled growth in cloud resources and costs, can pose challenges for an organization's financial stability. FinOps exists to prevent sprawl by establishing governance policies and controls to monitor, manage, and control cloud spending across teams and projects. FinOps provides organizations with the necessary tools and processes to identify and address instances of wasteful spending, redundant resources, or unoptimized configurations. What are the capabilities of FinOps? Effectively implemented, FinOps does more than simply realign organizational focus. It provides clear capabilities for businesses in regard to cloud financial management. These include the following: Accurate cost analysis FinOps allows organizations to more clearly track where their costs are coming from, comparing current and past spending to identify key drivers. Real-time decision making In a usage-based cloud environment, businesses need to be able to make precise predictions and split-second decisions regarding finances. FinOps generates real-time data insights, so organizations can respond quickly and accurately. Improved resource planning Effective planning and budgeting depend on a foreknowledge of what resources an organization will need, and when. Historical data analysis through FinOps helps businesses better forecast resource usage, for more-efficient planning. Budgeting should be detailed and combined across multiple vendors and resources and provide an awareness of where the organization is in relation to their goals and forcasts. What are the core principles of FinOps? As FinOps is largely dependent on team ownership and commitment, it relies heavily on self-governing behavior to promote accountability and business agility. With this in mind, FinOps is built on several core principles. Accountability By establishing clearly defined Objectives and Key Results (OKRs), Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), and other metrics, organizations ensure that teams understand their responsibility in optimizing the financial outcomes of their cloud usage. This encourages ownership, fosters a culture of responsibility, and drives continuous improvement in optimizing costs and delivering business value. Agility Agile practices enable flexibility, iterative improvements, and responsiveness in managing cloud costs, allowing organizations to allocate resources efficiently and adjust plans as necessary to optimize financial outcomes. Blamelessness Although accountability is a major principle in FinOps, finger-pointing is not. Mistakes are viewed as part of the learning journey and a fundamental part of the process improvement within the FinOps culture. Business-value based decisions Rather than depending on aggregate spending, businesses should focus on value-based metrics and unit economics. FinOps prompts conscious decision making that must often tradeoff between speed, cost, and quality. Capacity and resource planning Businesses must be keenly aware of their available resources and make a concerted effort to prioritize and allocate cloud resources effectively. Centralized management While buy-in must be organization-wide, FinOps should be driven by a centralized team that works with cloud providers to govern cloud finances. This the FinOps team to focus on multiple factors such as the usage, optimization, and securing better discounted rates. Collaboration The real-time accessibility provided by the cloud demands ongoing collaboration and continuous improvement and innovation between finance and technology teams. Cost Transparency By providing visibility into cloud spending and costs, organizations can make informed decisions, track usage patterns, and identify areas for optimization. Cost transparency facilitates collaboration among stakeholders, enables data-driven discussions, and helps align cloud spending with established business priorities. Governance and policy Businesses that incorporate FinOps must establish usage policies for all cloud resources. Defining who is authorized to use which cloud properties and when they use them will improve forecasting. Security Although nearly all cloud vendors provide some level of security, FinOps organizations must likewise take responsibility for security-related functions. This may include key management, duty segregation, risk management, and more. Shared ownership of cloud usage Resource usage and optimization is decentralized, putting the responsibility for managing cloud usage against an established budget in the hands of individual feature and product owners and teams. Timely and accessible reporting FinOps organizations must be capable of processing cost data as soon as it becomes available, improving visibility and driving faster feedback loops. Data and insights should be visible throughout every level of the organization, and performance should be assessed using industry peer-level benchmarking. Variable cost models Cloud-based technologies rely on variable costs, making agile, iterative cost planning much more effective than long-term forecasting. FinOps views this as an advantage, allowing organizations to continually optimize cloud costs by making ongoing adjustments and course corrections. What is the FinOps lifecycle? Because FinOps takes an iterative approach to managing cloud finances, the FinOps lifecycle can be visualized as an ongoing three-step process. Inform FinOps depends upon clear visibility into resources, budgeting, benchmarking, and more, to promote real-time decision making for businesses and teams. The more informed the organization is with visibility and allocation, the better they will be able to manage cloud costs. Optimize With relevant data in hand, the organization must next take action to reduce spend and right-size capacity without reducing cloud effectiveness. Optimization means taking a cold, hard look at utilization and rates, and making necessary changes. Operate After trimming away the excess, organizations need to assess effectiveness. Measuring speed, cost, and quality of cloud capacities, they compare results to predefined goals. As improvements are made and tested, the business continuously renews the cycle, for ongoing FinOps optimization. It's important to note that not only is this cycle self-repeating, it's also team dependent. An organization may find itself in multiple different stages at the same time, across various departments. Who are FinOps team members and stakeholders? Because FinOps is an organization-wide cultural shift that requires collaboration between many teams and departments, essentially most people within the organization are FinOps stakeholders. That said, those with the most vested interest in FinOps include the following: Executives Executives lead by example in embracing FinOps culture. They focus on accountability and transparency throughout the entire organization, and act as a safeguard against teams exceeding budgets. Key executives who are often involved with FinOps teams include the Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Chief Information Officer (CIO), and the Chief Financial Officer (CFO). Finance/procurement Finance and procurement professionals rely on accurate financial reporting and historic billing data to improve accounting and forecasting. They also use their analytical insights to negotiate rates with cloud vendors. Business/product owner Business/product owners take the lead in guiding new products, services, and features to the market, ensuring their successful adoption, and facilitating continuous growth year after year. These individuals are also expected to leverage their expertise to align cloud resources with business objectives and drive operational efficiency and reduce costs. Engineering/DevOps Engineering and operations teams work within FinOps to establish cost as a performance metric and are responsible for building and maintaining FinOps support services. They are often the highest consumers of cloud resources and therefore need to respond and optimize their solutions to minimize cloud spend. FinOps practitioners FinOps practitioners help forecast cloud spend, and work within teams to accurately budget and allocate resources. These FinOps practitioners often include individuals who are software asset managers that are performing similar tasks with enterprise software and SaaS solutions. What are the roles of FinOps Teams vs. Cloud Center of Excellence teams (CCoE)? FinOps teams are built around principles of agility, which allow for some flexibility in how FinOps teams are structured. They often include executives, FinOps practitioners, finance analysts or consultants, and members of stakeholder teams like Engineering and DevOps. That said, many organizations also find that a collaborative and cross-functional team called the Cloud Center of Excellence (CCoE) plays a pivotal role in overseeing strategy, governance, and best practices designed to drive business transformation through cloud utilization. The CCoE serves as a central hub, interacting with various departments and stakeholders across the organization. Think of this team as the front-end planners and strategists. Their primary responsibility is to manage and optimize the organization's cloud operations, ensuring alignment with business goals. By establishing and implementing cloud governance policies, the CCoE enables other teams to leverage standardized practices, maximize the benefits of the cloud, and facilitate the overall transformation of the business. The CCoE acts as a guiding force, providing expertise, support, and strategic direction to ensure the effective and efficient utilization of cloud resources throughout the organization. A FinOps team operates more as the back-end practitioners who monitor and account for the cloud practice and help optimize areas for better productivity and cost efficiencies. Both teams are necessary to mature your cloud management practices and results. And in some cases, especially where businesses are primarily in the cloud, FinOps may belong as a subgroup of the Cloud Center of Excellence. What are the key benefits of FinOps? By providing a reliable, agile approach to cloud finance management, FinOps offers a number of distinct advantages Real-time reporting Improved cost and resource visibility More-efficient workflows Better team collaboration Increased operational flexibility Cloud cost management and optimization Cost efficiency Resiliency Velocity Increased transparency Budgeting What FinOps metrics are important to track? Accountability This metric drives both the process and cultural transformation journey, aiming to foster financial accountability and accelerate the realization of business value. By streamlining IT financial processes and facilitating frictionless cloud governance, the accountability metric empowers organizations to take ownership of their cloud costs and optimize spending effectively. Reporting costs and consumption to executive management and individual departments is often referred to as “show-backs” or “chargebacks.” Benchmark performance The benchmark performance metric enables organizations to compare their cloud spending and cost optimization efforts against industry standards and peers. It involves analyzing OKRs and related KPIs, identifying what percentage of cloud spend has been budgeted for, and reviewing other relevant performance data to create a scorecard detailing how the organization's FinOps strategy measures up. Cost optimization The cost optimization metric focuses on strategic spending to maximize business value. This offers a consistent methodology for visualizing and managing cloud consumption in the most cost-effective ways. This metric empowers organizations to identify areas where costs can be reduced, resources may be optimized, and cloud spending can more-effectively align with predefined business objectives. Cost visibility Cost visibility emphasizes the importance of transparency and traceability in cloud-related expenses. Relying on well-defined resource hierarchy and project structure standards, and complemented by a labeling and tagging data architecture, this metric enables organizations to gain valuable insights into resource utilization and expenditure. Planning and forecasting This metric enables organizations to align their cloud usage with financial objectives, providing insights for budgeting, resource allocation, and informed decision-making. Planning and forecasting is typically based on historical-spending data, augmented with predictions based on upcoming initiatives. Tools and accelerators The tools and accelerators metric emphasizes the adoption of appropriate tools and technologies to enhance cost visibility, automate cost analysis, and provide actionable insights. These resources enable organizations to apply the full potential of FinOps to reach their goals, enabling better decision-making and cost optimization in the process. Total costs Total costs encompass not only the direct costs associated with cloud resources but also indirect costs such as data transfer fees, support charges, and any other expenses related to cloud usage. By considering the complete cost picture, organizations can accurately assess the financial impact of their cloud operations and make informed decisions regarding cost optimization and resource allocation. What are FinOps best practices for managing cloud spending? As previously addressed, FinOps is a cultural and operational shift that demands ongoing support and accountability throughout an entire organization. To help ensure FinOps success, here are several best practices that can be implemented across levels, teams, and departments. Determine where money is being spent Identify which applications, teams, and departments are using which resources. Visibility into current spending will provide a clear starting point for reducing costs without negatively impacting performance. Eliminate unnecessary costs As unnecessary costs are identified, cut them out. FinOps businesses need to be able to run lean, without any room for extraneous cloud expenses. Leverage discounted reserved cloud compute When reserved instances are available, consider purchasing them for future use. Reserved instances are often available at cheaper rates, and can help reduce costs when compared to on-demand options. But they need to be budgeted and used within a certain timeframe or you lose them, which can be even more costly. Employ autoscaling When workloads are unpredictable, take advantage of autoscaling options to automatically adjust computational resources to match active services. Avoid being locked into a single vendor By working with multiple vendors, businesses improve their flexibility and allow for a better range of cloud options. Plus, they can take advantage of different services and capabilities that match the objectives of your business service or application running in the cloud. Seek out and take advantage of discounts While it can be advantageous to work with a range of vendors, some vendors offer volume discounts, potentially offering significant savings on cloud services. Launch Deploy FinOps solutions gradually, starting with foundational changes. Build enthusiasm and momentum by ensuring that everything is operating as expected and that successes are being clearly documented. Optimize resource utilization and foster a culture of cost-conscious operations, adjusting where necessary. How should an organization implement a FinOps program? Implementing a FinOps program involves several key steps that span from planning to launch. By following these steps, organizations can successfully adopt and leverage the FinOps framework to optimize cloud costs and drive financial accountability. Here is a brief guide on implementing a FinOps program: Plan for FinOps adoption Begin by researching and understanding the pain points, operational challenges, and interdepartmental dynamics within the organization. Assemble a pilot team of engineers, finance, and C-Suite representatives. Collaboratively brainstorm a vision for the desired outcomes and consider seeking guidance from external consultants to help shape the plan. Take guidance from the CCoE team, if there is one in place. Conduct analysis Conduct a comprehensive analysis of cloud expenses to gain deeper visibility into current IT budgets and allocations by team. This stage involves examining cost breakdowns, identifying drivers, and understanding the utilization patterns of various cloud resources. The analysis phase provides valuable insights into the current state of cloud spending and serves as a basis for developing targeted cost-saving strategies. Introduce FinOps to the organization Communicate the FinOps framework clearly and engage the entire organization, preparing teams for the cultural and operational shift that will be required. To ensure FinOps success, promote a shared understanding of values and routines that need improvement to embrace a cost-conscious mindset. Prepare for launch Establish measurable OKRs and associated KPIs to track progress. Create a roadmap outlining the progression of the FinOps adoption journey from initial stages (Crawl) to scaling up (Walk) and achieving a mature, optimized state (Run). Launch Deploy FinOps solutions gradually, starting with foundational changes. Build enthusiasm and momentum by ensuring that everything is operating as expected and that successes are being clearly documented. Optimize resource utilization and foster a culture of cost-conscious operations, adjusting where necessary. Perform benchmarking Measure the performance of cloud instances by comparing resource utilization, performance metrics, and costs against industry standards and internal benchmarks. By analyzing this data, FinOps teams can identify instances where resources are underutilized or over-provisioned, negatively impacting cost efficiency across the organization. Optimize moving forward Optimization is an ongoing stage that permeates the entire FinOps process. This involves various strategies, such as rightsizing instances to match workload demands and business hours, leveraging auto-scaling capabilities, repositioning workloads to cost-effective cloud services, and adopting containerization or serverless architectures (where applicable). Continuous optimization efforts ensure that cloud resources are used efficiently, costs are minimized, and the desired level of performance is achieved without unnecessary overspending. Learn more about HPE About us Leadership Corporate responsibility Awards and recognition Careers Our latest HPE Discover Events Customer successes Newsroom Technology Leadership HPE Labs AI Digital Sovereignty Quantum Security More resources Contact Communities Education Partners HPE Glossary Overview HPE Glossary Overview HPE Glossary Overview FinOps (Financial Operations) What is FinOps? FinOps (Financial Operations), a cultural practice and operational framework, helps organizations maximize the value of cloud and technology investments. It combines technical, financial, and business teams to create faster, smarter cloud usage and budget decisions. It encourages organizations to be accountable for their cloud costs, understand their decisions, and collaborate to improve efficiency without sacrificing speed or creativity. FinOps simplifies cost control, waste reduction, and technology spend alignment by integrating real-time data and established objectives. Explore HPE FinOps solutions Time to read: 8 min 02 seconds | Updated: February 5, 2026 Table of Contents Why are FinOps important? Cost management and financial accountability: FinOps controls cloud expenditure, prevents budget overruns, and promotes team accountability for cloud usage and expenses. Optimization of cloud resources: FinOps helps firms reduce waste, improve resource allocation, and make cost-effective cloud efficiency decisions. Facilitated collaboration: FinOps fosters finance, operations, and engineering collaboration for better cloud management and decision-making. Real-time visibility and agility: With real-time insights into cloud consumption, FinOps enables enterprises to react rapidly, align spending with business objectives, and respond to market developments. Strategic planning and forecasting: FinOps helps firms' budget and plan for future cloud investments, improving forecasting and cost management. Compliance and governance: FinOps reduces compliance risks and maintains cloud expenditure governance by following policies and regulations. What are the key principles of FinOps? The key principles of FinOps are essential for managing and optimizing cloud spending and promoting team collaboration. They oversee data-driven, accountable cloud investments that support corporate goals. Team collaboration: Helps engineering, finance, and business teams to make informed cloud usage and cost decisions. User and cost ownership: Assigns responsibility for cloud spend to the teams consuming resources, encouraging cost-conscious operations. Financial accountability: Connects cloud expenses to business results for transparency and disciplined expenditure. Real-time decision making: Follows live data and insights to optimize cloud performance and cost. Accessible, actionable data: Gives stakeholders clear, precise, and real-time cost data for decision-making. Continuous improvement: Promotes cloud cost management monitoring, analysis, and optimization. Alignment with business goals: Every cloud investment should support strategic goals, including faster delivery, innovation, and customer experience. Leveraging cloud flexibility: Makes the most of the cloud's elastic nature by only paying for the resources consumed. How is FinOps expanding beyond the public cloud, and what strategies can organizations use to unify technology spend optimization? FinOps scopes for a broader horizon FinOps was initially created to manage public cloud infrastructure expenses, but its principles now encompass a broader range of technology spending. The FinOps Foundation has added "Cloud+" scopes to its framework to reflect its relevance wherever technology spend occurs. The FinOps Framework's principles of openness, accountability, and optimization can be applied to environments beyond public cloud providers with this expansion. FinOps for SaaS FinOps concepts are crucial in SaaS. As documented by the FinOps Foundation, the challenges of managing public cloud spending are often mirrored in how SaaS resources are acquired frequently through decentralized, individual-level procurement using corporate credit cards. This usually results in limited organizational visibility into costs and usage. The FinOps approach for SaaS addresses these challenges by bringing financial transparency and accountability to software spending. It involves analyzing varied pricing models such as license-based, per user, or consumption-based to ensure that organizations are paying only for the services they truly utilize. Companies can track SaaS prices, monitor consumption, and cut costs with the iterative FinOps Framework Capabilities. FinOps for the data center The data center scope represents a vital and growing area for the FinOps discipline. Data centers have traditionally used an upfront purchase model, but now options are available to shift to a consumption-based usage and cost model. This allows FinOps Practitioners to work with others to evolve their organization to more collaborative spending habits. Applying FinOps to the data center means bringing the same discipline of cost transparency and accountability to on-premises and hybrid environments. This includes optimizing server utilization, managing virtualization costs, and planning for hardware refresh cycles. For companies with a robust data center presence, such as those that partner with HPE, this scope is essential. It allows them to apply cloud-like financial discipline to their entire estate, ensuring they can make informed decisions about their technology investments, both in the cloud and in their own data center. GreenLake Flex Solutions and other as-a-service solutions can help an organization establish a FinOps practice for their data center. FinOps for the hybrid world: unifying your strategy Beyond managing individual scopes like public cloud, SaaS, and data centers, the most forward-thinking organizations are adopting a holistic, hybrid FinOps approach. This is where the true power of the discipline lies. In a world where IT environments are a complex mix of on-premises infrastructure and multiple public cloud providers, FinOps serves as the unifying layer. A key challenge is gaining "single-pane-of-glass" visibility across all these disparate environments. By implementing a consistent FinOps strategy, including standardized tagging and cost allocation models, teams can make objective, data-driven decisions on where to place workloads for optimal cost and performance. This unified approach not only helps manage the complexity of hybrid IT but also enables organizations to strategically leverage HPE's on-premises and private cloud solutions, ensuring that every dollar spent on technology is driving maximum business value. What key capabilities make FinOps successful in cloud and hybrid IT? FinOps capabilities: The building blocks of a FinOps practice To manage a successful FinOps practice, a business must create fundamental competencies. More than people and processes, FinOps platforms use automation and analytics. The FinOps Framework establishes these domains and capabilities that enable mature, data-driven financial operations across cloud and hybrid IT.
Understand usage & cost This domain is about visibility—knowing what you spend and why. All other FinOps actions depend on it. Allocation: Assigning technology costs accurately to teams, applications, or business units. Anomaly management: Identifying and responding to unusual anomalies before they become budget overruns. Data ingestion: Unifying cloud, SaaS, and on-premises pricing and use data. Reporting & analytics: Tracking usage and spending patterns with reporting and other data visualizations to inform cost optimization.
Optimize usage & cost Once visibility is in place, the focus shifts to efficiency—using resources smarter without compromising business performance. Workload optimization: Matching resources to demand. HPE's FinOps solutions recommend VM sizes and settings to avoid over-or under-provisioning. Rate optimization: Reducing unit costs via reserved instances or savings schemes. Architecting for cloud: Embedding FinOps ideas into technical architectures from the start to reduce costs. Cloud sustainability Licensing & SaaS
Quantify business value This domain connects technology consumption to business outcomes, enabling firms to prioritize investment based on value. Budgeting: Setting and tracking team, application, and project spending. Forecasting: Utilizing historical data and usage trends to plan financial futures. Unit economics: Relating expenses to business factors like transaction and customer costs to show how technology spending supports business goals. Benchmarking Planning & Estimating
Manage the FinOps Practice These are the organizational levers that sustain and scale FinOps as a cross-functional discipline. FinOps education & enablement: Equipping finance, engineering, and business teams to participate in a culture of responsibility. Invoicing and chargeback: Internal billing to assign consumption to teams. Automated chargeback and invoicing in hybrid environments promote accountability with HPE Morpheus. Policy & governance: Setting rules, guardrails, and compliance mechanisms to match technology use with financial and business goals. FinOps assessment FinOps practice operations Intersecting disciplines Onboarding workloads How can HPE help you with FinOps? In the following ways HPE Supports FinOps:
FinOps tools Unified hybrid cloud view and insights: the consumption analytics capability of GreenLake delivers a single view for normalized usage and cost data across GreenLake as-a-service offerings, AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. It offers customizable dashboards, robust showback capabilities, proactive cost optimization recommendations and anomaly detection, cost forecasting, and FOCUS exports to support chargeback mechanisms. Workload-focused reporting and governance: HPE Morpheus Enterprise Software provides cost reporting with tagging that also extends into its control plane to help you implement rightsizing and enforce governance over the resources that HPE Morpheus Enterprise orchestrates.
Cultural & process transformation Advisory & professional services: HPE experts help embed financial responsibility into cloud operations, guide strategy, and build FinOps capabilities. People-process-technology alignment: Promotes collaboration between engineering, finance, and business teams for shared accountability. Accountability & efficiency: Links cost data to accounting and budgeting, enabling ongoing efficiency improvements.
Flexible consumption & financial services As-a-service infrastructure: Consumption-based pricing with GreenLake Flex Solutions and other offerings aligns IT costs directly with business outcomes, improving predictability. IT asset lifecycle solutions: HPE Financial Services offers lifecycle management, capital release, and flexible financing to fund IT strategically while controlling costs. How does FinOps differ from traditional IT financial management? FinOps redefines financial management for the cloud era, filling in the gaps left by traditional IT finance management. Traditional methods work for static, on-premises infrastructure but not for dynamic, pay-as-you-go cloud computing. FinOps is designed for this environment, enabling cost optimization, cross-functional communication, cloud spending and business alignment. FAQs What is the first step to implement FinOps? The first step is to define a clear vision, strategy, and roadmap and stand up a cross-functional FinOps team to drive maturity. Begin by documenting objectives (cost optimization, unit economics, and accountability), nominating stakeholders (FinOps lead, engineering, cloud operations, finance, and product), setting KPIs (cost per workload, 30-day burn rate, and reserved instance coverage), and creating a phased roadmap. Make cloud spend visible immediately by enabling tagging, exporting billing data, and building cost allocation of dashboards—accurate visibility is the primary driver and justification for adopting FinOps. What are the most common challenges of FinOps? Common challenges include a lack of accurate, timely cloud cost visibility due to poor tagging or allocation; difficulty aligning engineering, finance, and product teams on shared cost accountability; and resistance to culture change from traditional procurement models. Other issues are unpredictable usage patterns that impact forecasting, complex pricing models from multiple cloud providers, limited automation for cost optimization, and immature unit-economics tracking. Ensuring real-time data, governance, and cross-functional collaboration is essential to overcoming these challenges and driving FinOps maturity. How do you measure the success of FinOps practice? Measure FinOps success using these KPI categories: Enabling/adoption metrics (coverage and data quality): Percentage of infrastructure reported, percentage of resources tagged, percentage of unallocated cost, freshness of billing exports, and time to cost reconciliation. Outcome metrics (financial and efficiency results): forecast vs. actual variance, forecasting accuracy (MAE/MAPE), reservation/savings-plan utilization and coverage, cost per workload/user/transaction (unit economics), waste reclaimed, and cost-avoidance from optimizations. Overall success should be assessed by accurate forecasting relative to actuals and improved engineering economic efficiency (lower unit costs and more predictable spend). What is "unit economics" in the context of FinOps? Unit economics in FinOps is the practice of mapping cloud costs to a measurable productivity outcome that represents value delivery. Teams attribute cost to a unit of value—for example, cost per transaction, API call, active user, feature, ML inference, or customer segment—and track cost per unit over time. This productivity outcome is an intermediary tying infrastructure spend to business metrics (revenue per user, CAC, and churn). Clear unit economics enable informed trade-offs between cost and value, create engineering accountability, improve forecasting, and guide decisions on optimization vs. investment. What is the role of engineers and developers in FinOps? Engineers and developers play a critical role in FinOps by using cost visibility, insights, and best practices from the FinOps team to inform architecture and design choices. They align resource usage with business value, optimize workloads for efficiency, choose appropriate services and pricing models, and eliminate waste. By integrating cost awareness into development and deployment processes, they improve unit metrics (for example, cost per user, request, or transaction) and ensure engineering decisions advance both technical performance and financial efficiency. Is FinOps just another name for cloud cost optimization? Cloud cost optimization describes specific tactics—rightsizing instances, removing idle resources, and so on. FinOps is a broader cultural practice that brings together finance, technology, and product stakeholders to collaboratively and continuously manage cloud spending and maximize business value. How does FinOps work in a multi-cloud or hybrid cloud environment? Cross-platform visibility is essential in multi-cloud and hybrid environments. Costs, usage, and performance must be captured and normalized across public clouds, private clouds, and on-premises systems to enable accurate allocation, unit economics, and optimization. Consistent tagging and reporting across all endpoints allow unified governance, forecasting, and meaningful savings comparisons. FinOps principles—cost transparency, unit-cost tracking, and cross-functional optimization—also apply to non-cloud environments (bare metal, data centers, and SaaS). Streamline your cloud costs and drive business value effectively. Published on 18 December 2025 Blog Summarize: ChatGPT Perplexity AI FinOps – What is FinOps & Cloud FinOps? In the rapidly evolving landscape of cloud computing, managing costs effectively while maximizing business value has become crucial. This challenge has led to the rise of FinOps, or Financial Operations, a practice designed to bring financial accountability to the variable spending model of cloud services. FinOps not only helps control costs but also enhances decision-making across cross-functional teams by balancing speed, cost, and quality. What is FinOps? FinOps is a business approach that combines finance, operations, and technology to manage and optimize cloud spending effectively. It's a set of practices designed to help teams get the most value out of cloud services by making informed decisions based on financial and operational data. This approach fosters collaboration among different departments, promoting transparency and accountability in cloud investments. The goal of FinOps is to enable companies to control costs while maximizing cloud efficiency and innovation. The Growing Importance of FinOps Beyond mere cost management, FinOps represents a cultural shift towards comprehensive understanding and real-time management of cloud expenses. It empowers organizations to make decisions that are closely tied to business outcomes, thereby maximizing the impact of their cloud investments. What Does FinOps Stand For? The core of FinOps revolves around the principle of visibility, optimization, and control. By enhancing visibility into cloud expenditures, organizations can anticipate and manage their financial operations more effectively. Optimization involves both cost savings and maximizing the value derived from cloud investments. It ensures that every dollar spent is fully justified and directly tied to advancing business objectives. Control means implementing governance and accountability to sustain these financial management practices across all departments. Understanding Cloud FinOps Cloud FinOps specifically addresses the unique challenges associated with the dynamic and often unpredictable costs of cloud services. Managing and optimizing these costs requires a robust strategy that integrates financial management with technical insights. Key Components of FinOps in Cloud Environments Cost Allocation and Reporting: Tools that provide detailed cost reporting and chargeback capabilities are essential. They help allocate costs accurately to the departments or projects driving them, which in turn promotes accountability and can influence more efficient usage behaviors. Real-Time Decision Making: Real-time analytics provide immediate insights into spending trends and anomalies, enabling quick adjustments and proactive budget management. Optimization and Waste Reduction: Identifying underutilized resources and ensuring they are resized or eliminated is crucial for cost efficiency. Automation plays a significant role here, helping to scale down or terminate resources that are not in active use. How FinOps and SAM Work Together While FinOps and Software Asset Management (SAM) address different aspects of IT cost optimization, they share a common goal: delivering financial visibility and control across technology investments. FinOps focuses on managing and optimizing cloud resources and spending, while SAM governs software licensing, compliance, and usage across on-premise and SaaS environments. Together, they form a complete view of an organization's digital asset landscape. FinOps provides real-time financial insights into cloud consumption, and SAM ensures that every application—whether cloud-based or on-premise—is licensed, utilized, and compliant. When aligned, these practices help organizations balance cost efficiency with governance and risk control. Xensam's platform supports both disciplines by providing deep visibility into software and cloud assets, normalizing data across environments, and integrating usage insights that power accurate financial and operational decisions. This synergy between SAM and FinOps enables IT, finance, and operations teams to collaborate around a single source of truth for technology spending. Benefits of Implementing FinOps Implementing FinOps provides several advantages that help companies manage their cloud spending more effectively. It improves cost transparency by offering clear visibility into what drives costs and how they are allocated across the cloud infrastructure. This approach fosters enhanced collaboration by bridging the gap between finance, operations, and development teams, promoting a shared understanding of financial goals. Additionally, FinOps increases agility, allowing businesses to scale resources up or down based on current needs and financial strategies without compromising service quality. Overall, FinOps helps organizations get more value from their cloud resources, ensuring that spending aligns with business objectives. FinOps Tools and Strategies Implementing FinOps successfully involves using a variety of tools and strategies to enhance cost management and accountability: Budget Management Tools: These are software solutions that help forecast, track, and manage cloud expenditures. These tools help in maintaining a grip on financial flows and preventing budget overruns. Cost Optimization Platforms: Tools that analyze consumption patterns and recommend cost-saving measures. These platforms can pinpoint inefficiencies and propose optimizations to ensure that every dollar spent is truly necessary. Governance Frameworks: Guidelines that ensure compliance with financial policies and promote cost accountability. Transform Your Cloud Spending with Xensam At Xensam, we integrate leading FinOps practices to ensure that your cloud investments are economically sound and strategically aligned with your broader business goals. Our platform leverages advanced AI-driven software normalization and real-time inventory management to enhance the accuracy and effectiveness of cloud asset management. This enables businesses to not only track and manage their cloud investments but also optimize their software and hardware assets across various environments. Comprehensive Software Asset Management: Xensam's platform provides a holistic view of your software assets, including 500,000+ on-premise and SaaS applications, each enriched with metadata attributes like license requirements, release dates, end-of-life information, upgrade paths, and GDPR compliance. This vast library ensures that businesses can manage software assets with unparalleled precision. Optimized SaaS Management: Our tools simplify SaaS management by offering robust web app inventory capabilities, license portal integrations, and cost optimization analysis. By delivering detailed insights into your SaaS environment, Xensam helps you identify potential savings and make informed decisions about software use and adjustments needed to align with your financial and operational goals. Enhanced Security and Compliance: With Xensam's Security Center, businesses gain a comprehensive overview of security vulnerabilities and potential legal incompliance associated with their software assets. This proactive approach not only safeguards against security risks but also ensures that all cloud spending adheres to compliance standards. Effective Cost Management: Xensam's Cost Center consolidates all software-related costs into one place, offering businesses a granular breakdown of expenses. This visibility empowers you to understand where and how funds are being allocated and identifies opportunities for cost-saving that do not compromise the service quality or business growth. Enterprise-Level Scalability: Managing complex software portfolios, especially in data centers and large enterprises involving heavyweights like Oracle Database and IBM server software, is streamlined thanks to our advanced license algorithms and AI-driven normalization. This ensures that even the most complex licensing scenarios are handled efficiently, allowing for scalability without financial waste. Active Usage Insights: Understanding the actual usage of applications can dramatically impact cost-efficiency in cloud environments. Xensam provides detailed metrics on active usage versus mere open applications, distinguishing between software metering and active engagement to ensure that investments are made in resources that truly benefit the organization's operational needs. By integrating Xensam's FinOps solutions, organizations can transform their approach to cloud spending from a reactive cost center to a proactive strategic asset. Our platform not only enhances financial accountability and operational efficiency but also supports dynamic scalability and strategic business alignment.
